title: Cross and crucifix
hook: an empty cross, or Christ on it: churches choose differently

segments.voice: Yesterday, candles: a small flame that keeps going after you've walked out the door. Your line was a prayer left burning.

On a jeweler's tray, two silver necklaces, same chain, same shape. One is a plain cross: two bars, nothing else. The other carries a tiny figure, arms stretched wide, head bowed. In one church, the big cross above the altar has that figure on it. Across the street, the cross on the wall is bare wood. Nobody in either building forgot anything. Each one chose. And the two choices say the same sentence, with the stress on different words.
screen: `ONE CHURCH: A FIGURE. ONE CHURCH: BARE WOOD.`

segments.voice: Day eighteen asked why an execution became the sign on the steeple. Today, two ways of showing it. First, the plain difference. A crucifix is a cross with the figure of Christ on it; a cross on its own has nobody on it. Both point at the same death, an execution the letter to the Hebrews places outside the city gate. That's the strange thing: an instrument of death ended up on necklaces and steeples. Paul wrote to the Galatians: "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." Next, the crucifix. Catholic churches keep one on or near the altar, and Orthodox Christians often use crosses with Christ painted on them, like an icon. Paul told the church in Corinth: "For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified." Some who pray before a crucifix say it keeps the cost in view: a real body, real nails, nothing tidied away. Then the empty cross. In other churches, Protestant ones especially, the cross is bare. To those who choose it, the emptiness is the message. In Matthew, the women come to the tomb at dawn, and the angel says: "He is not here: for he is risen, as he said." The bare cross points to that morning. Last, side by side. Churches with a crucifix still sing about the empty tomb; churches with a bare cross still read the story of the nails. One story: one holds the death in view, the other the morning after. In both, the whole sentence gets said: he died, and he rose.
screen: `AN INSTRUMENT OF DEATH, WORN ON A CHAIN.`
`THE BARE CROSS: HE IS NOT HERE.`

segments.voice: Look at a cross, a necklace, a picture, a steeple out the window, or the one on the screen, and notice first whether it's empty or carries a figure. Let your eyes move slowly along the upright beam, the crossbeam, the place where the two meet. If you pray, you can pray in the words your own church uses before a cross; if you don't, simply look, and let it be a shape that carries a story.
Cross and crucifix. The bare shape, and the shape with Christ on it: two ways of showing one story.
Your line: he died, he rose. Two shapes, one sentence. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: Why do some churches have Jesus on the cross, and others just a plain one?
options: Both tell one story: a crucifix keeps his death in view, a bare cross points to the empty tomb.
A bare cross means that church doesn't dwell on his death or read about the nails at all.
They mark two separate beliefs: one church says Jesus died, the other says he rose again.
chat.meaning: One holds the death in view, the other the morning after. Both kinds of church say the whole sentence: he died, and he rose.
